implementation_notes: C++23 gives the effect-like contexts their map: opt.transform(f) invokes f only when the optional holds a value and returns std::optional<U> - an empty optional is passed through without calling f - and exp.transform(f) does the same for std::expected while preserving the error value; cppreference notes explicitly that 'some languages call this operation map'. Because the result object is constructed in place, transform also replaces the hand-written `o ? std::optional{f(*o)} : std::nullopt` conditional and the copy it performed. Change the error channel with transform_error, sequence with and_then, and recover with or_else. Keep the classic form only where the project pins C++17 or a library without the monadic operations.
pitfalls: transform requires the callable to return a non-reference, non-array object type: mapping to a reference (a member, a container element) does not compile - return a pointer, a std::reference_wrapper, or use a view instead.

The monadic members exist only since C++23: on C++17 the operation is hand-written under an if, and the classic mistakes - default-constructing the target, copying the payload first - are exactly what transform removes.
transform maps the value channel only: use transform_error for the error, and and_then (not transform) when the callable itself returns an optional or expected, or the result nests.

variants.name: Range pipeline via std::views::transform (C++20)
variants.implementation_notes: For sequence-shaped contexts C++20 makes map a view: r | std::views::transform(f) yields a transform_view that applies f lazily as it is iterated and models the properties of the underlying range - cppreference describes it as 'a view of a sequence that applies a transformation function to each element', with views::transform as the adaptor object. It replaces the eager std::transform-into-an-output-iterator form and allocates no intermediate container, and the same vocabulary continues with filter/take so a whole pipeline maps and selects without owning a result. Materialise deliberately when the result is reused (std::ranges::to in C++23, ranges::copy), and keep the classic std::transform algorithm on C++11/14/17 code or where one fused pass measures faster.
pitfalls: Views are non-owning and lazy: captured references (a temporary container, a local, a dangling range) must outlive the view, and iterating twice re-runs the function, side effects included.
The callable must be copy-constructible and regular-invocable with the range's reference type: a move-only or reference-returning lambda does not satisfy transform_view's constraints.
views::transform and the eager ranges::transform algorithm are different overload sets with confusingly similar names and errors; pick one form per pipeline and materialise explicitly.

variants.name: Hand-written fmap / Functor trait over the project's own contexts (C++11)
variants.idiom_name: non-member fmap(f, F<A>) specialised per context (typeclass emulation)
variants.implementation_notes: Where the contexts are the project's own types (a Result, a parser, a task wrapper) and the toolchain predates the standard library's transform members, the operation is declared once as a non-member fmap and overloaded - or dispatched through a Functor<F> trait class with one specialisation per context - which is the typeclass emulation used by functional C++ libraries and the only way to pass the operation to generic code as a template parameter. The full structure is hand-written: the trait, the per-context specialisation, the return-type computation (decltype / trailing return), and the law tests. Keep it when several contexts share helpers and the codebase can afford a second vocabulary beside std::transform; for a single context a plain member function is smaller and needs no trait.
pitfalls: Not every context can be partially specialised directly; teams end up wrapping it in a tag type (Kind<F, A>-style) just to dispatch, which changes the type users see and write in signatures.
Template errors for a missing instance land deep inside the trait machinery, and the laws stay untested unless a small suite covers each specialisation.

fmap is found by argument-dependent lookup: the instance for a third-party context must live in that context's namespace, and a misplaced specialisation produces 'no matching function' rather than 'no instance'.
